lines.text: The homeland of the Liberator, a country of mountains, plains and some of the richest oil fields on Earth. This is the story of Venezuela.
In 1567 the Spanish founded Caracas in a green valley near the Caribbean coast. It would become the capital.
Francisco de Miranda was born there in 1750. He fought in both the American and French revolutions, and dreamed of freeing his own land.
Andres Bello, poet and lawyer, was born in Caracas in 1781, and taught a young boy who would change a continent.
That boy was Simon Bolivar. Born in 1783, he would lead armies that freed much of South America from Spain, and be honoured as the Liberator.
In 1810 the fight against Spain began. It would last thirteen hard years.
On the fifth of July 1811 Venezuela declared itself free, the first land in Spanish America to do so.
So the nation of Venezuela was born, though its independence still had to be won on the battlefield.
In 1819 Bolivar joined Venezuela with Colombia, Ecuador and Panama into one great republic, Gran Colombia. Within about a decade, rivalries broke it apart.
In 1821, on the plain of Carabobo, Bolivar won the battle that secured Venezuela's independence.
A century of strongmen followed. Juan Vicente Gomez, born in 1857, would rule as dictator for almost thirty years and open the country to the oil companies.
Romulo Betancourt, born in 1908, would fight those dictators, and become known as the father of Venezuelan democracy.
In 1914 the first commercial oil well came in at Zumaque. Oil would shape everything that followed.
In 1933 a pilot named Jimmie Angel flew over a waterfall in the southern jungle. Angel Falls is the highest in the world.
Hugo Chavez was born in 1954 on the plains. He would rule from 1999 and lead what he called the Bolivarian revolution.
Nicolas Maduro, born in 1962, would be his successor, and under his rule the economy collapsed.
Maria Corina Machado, born in 1967, would lead the opposition against him, and win the Nobel Peace Prize in 2025.
In 1975 El Sistema began teaching music to poor children for free. Its orchestras gave the world the conductor Gustavo Dudamel.
That same decade the state took over the oil industry, and PDVSA became the company that ran it.
In 1989 sudden price rises set off riots in Caracas. The Caracazo was put down with great loss of life.
Three years later a young officer, Hugo Chavez, tried to seize power. The coup failed, but it made him famous.
In the years after he took office, more and more Venezuelans began to leave. In time, some eight million would go.
From the 2010s the economy fell apart, with runaway prices and empty shelves, and the exodus became one of the largest in the world.
In July 2024 Maduro claimed victory in a presidential election, but the opposition's own count showed Edmundo Gonzalez ahead.
The land of Bolivar still waits for the freedom he fought for.
